remote-cache.title: Remote track cache
remote-cache.body:
When you prepare cues on a track that lives on a paired computer (Library → remote library → Prepare cues), rave-mate first pulls a byte-exact copy of that audio file over the LAN peer link and keeps it in this cache. The cue editor - waveform, beatgrid, audition playback - then runs entirely against the local copy, so scrubbing stays instant even over slow Wi-Fi; only your saved cue changes travel back to the peer.

Each entry is keyed by peer, source path and the file's modification time: if the track changes on the peer, the stale copy is dropped and a fresh one is pulled on the next open. The cache trims itself to the size cap set here - least-recently-used copies are deleted first once the total exceeds the cap. The file currently being pulled is never trimmed; set the cap to 0 to use the built-in default (4096 MB).

Clearing the cache is always safe: it holds only replaceable copies, never originals or your cue edits - any track you open again is simply pulled from its peer again. On disk it lives in the remote_cache folder inside rave-mate's data directory (Open cache folder shows it).

remote-library.title: Remote library (paired instance)
remote-library.body:
You are looking at the OTHER computer's Library tab - the paired instance renders its own Library exactly as it would in its own window and streams the picture here; every click, key and edit you make is sent back and executed over there. Its own visible window is not touched or moved while you work.

Because commands execute on the remote machine, everything operates on ITS music files and database: beatgrid analysis (gridfix), cue and drop edits, tag writes, transcodes and playlist changes all read and write the remote library, using the remote computer's CPU/GPU and disk. Nothing is copied to this machine except the on-screen picture and small images like covers and waveforms.

Audio auditions (play/cue preview) start the REMOTE player - the sound comes out of the remote computer's audio device, not this one. That is by design: a booth laptop can prep the studio PC's library while the studio PC's monitors stay authoritative. Embedded video previews may be unavailable in remote mode.

If the link drops mid-session this banner turns amber and the view freezes; the remote side cleans its session up automatically. Reconnect (or re-select the peer in the Controlling switcher) to resume. Pairing and transport ride the same end-to-end-authenticated LAN peer link as the rest of rave-mate (Ed25519 + per-frame MACs) - nothing goes through the internet.

camera-paths.body:
VRChat's in-game camera records dolly paths - keyframe sequences (position, facing, speed, focus) the camera flies through smoothly. VRChat saves them as JSON files; rave-mate finds them, groups them by the world they were recorded in, and can back them up, organize them and re-load them.

The preview shows the path in 3D: each dot is a keyframe, the small violet line is the camera's facing, and the line colour encodes speed (mint = slow, pink = fast). The amber marker flies the path at its real recorded speed.

"Load into VRChat" sends the file over OSC so it appears in the in-game camera immediately - OSC must be enabled in VRChat (Action menu → Options → OSC). Loop and path-type aren't stored in the file; set them once in VRChat after loading.

“Play path” previews the flythrough right here: the viewer camera rides the path first-person at its recorded per-segment timing.
camera-paths.title: VRChat camera paths

dmx-connect.body:
DMX is the standard lighting-control protocol: 512 dimmer values (channels) per 'universe'. Art-Net carries those universes over the network as UDP on port 6454.

In your lighting software (a console, QLC+, xLights, ...) add an Art-Net output node, point it at this machine's IP address (or broadcast), universe number as below, and start sending. rave-mate also answers Art-Net discovery polls, so many consoles list it automatically.
dmx-connect.title: DMX / Art-Net

dmx-reemit.body: Forwards every universe received here back out over Art-Net - chain rave-mate in front of another machine or lighting tool that also needs the DMX feed. Sent at max 44 packets/s per universe with a 1/s keep-alive, per the Art-Net spec.
dmx-reemit.title: Art-Net re-emit

dmx-vrsl.body: VRSL (VR Stage Lighting) is the standard for club lighting in VRChat: light values are encoded as pixel blocks in the video stream, and the world's shaders decode them back into lights. rave-mate renders that pixel grid directly - no extra grid tool needed. Capture it in OBS, stream it, and a VRSL-enabled world lights up.
dmx-vrsl.title: VRSL pixel grid

dual-alignment.body:
When one set was captured twice - the broadcast audio (Icecast receiver) AND an OBS video recording - the two files rarely start at the same moment: you hit record and broadcast at different times, so the same beat sits at different positions in each file.

Alignment finds that time offset by listening to both recordings: each file's loudness envelope (how the energy rises and falls, ~50 times a second) is extracted with ffmpeg, and the two envelopes are cross-correlated - slid against each other until they match best. The confidence score says how decisively the best match beat every other position; "high" means the recordings clearly share the same audio.

Once aligned, both waveforms render on one shared timeline and a single IN/OUT range cuts BOTH files at the same real-world moment - so the exported audio and video have identical content and length. If the automatic result looks wrong (e.g. the video's audio is heavily processed), nudge the offset manually or type it directly; your manual value is kept until you re-run Auto-align.
dual-alignment.title: Audio ⇆ video time alignment

embedded-video.body:
The video plays right here, inside the app: rave-mate streams the file to its own window over a private localhost connection (HTTP with Range requests, so seeking is instant - the player fetches only the bytes it needs). Nothing leaves your machine and no extra player window opens.

The waveform below is the video's AUDIO track, analyzed exactly like an audio recording - navigate a multi-hour video by the music: click the waveform to seek, use the track dropdown to jump to a tracklist entry. When a set has both an audio capture and a video recording, the video runs as a muted, time-aligned preview while the (usually cleaner) broadcast audio plays - switch the source with the AUDIO/VIDEO toggle.

Decoding uses the app's web engine (Chromium): H.264/AAC MP4 - what OBS records by default - and WebM/VP9 play natively. An exotic codec or container shows an honest error instead; export a web-friendly cut via the encode presets, or open the file in your system player.
embedded-video.title: Embedded video playback

enc-audio-codec.body:
Copy keeps the original audio stream (bitrate, sample-rate, channel and loudness changes do not apply); None disables audio.

Lossless: FLAC preserves quality, its bitrate follows the source and compression level; PCM is uncompressed and ignores bitrate settings. Lossy: AAC is broadly compatible with a practical ceiling around 320 kbps; Opus is the most efficient, generous for stereo music at modest bitrates; Vorbis can go higher than AAC; MP3 CBR tops out at 320 kbps, while V0 VBR often sounds transparent with smaller files.

Each codec has a suggested bitrate for the source and a useful ceiling - above the ceiling, bigger files add no audible quality.
enc-audio-codec.title: Audio codec

enc-container.body:
The container is the file wrapper - it decides which video/audio codec combinations are valid.

MP4 is the safest delivery container: H.264/H.265/AV1 video with AAC-style audio compatibility. WebM is browser-friendly for open codecs: VP9 or AV1 video with Opus/Vorbis audio. MKV accepts nearly every codec; useful for archives and remuxes, less universal for playback.

Audio-only containers: Ogg is usually Vorbis or Opus and allows higher lossy audio ceilings than AAC. MP3 is universally playable, capped at 320 kbps for CBR. M4A/AAC is broadly compatible; AAC's practical top bitrate is 320 kbps. WAV/AIFF are uncompressed PCM: large files, no lossy bitrate control. FLAC is lossless compression: smaller than WAV, still bit-perfect. Opus is very efficient at lower bitrates.
enc-container.title: Container format

enc-loudness.body:
Normalize loudness applies one whole-track volume change - no compression. It is two-pass and fully transparent: pass 1 measures the whole track (EBU R128 integrated loudness + true peak), pass 2 applies ONE constant gain to the entire track - no compression, limiting or dynamics processing, so the mix and transients stay untouched. Gain up is capped so the true peak never exceeds the ceiling (a track that cannot reach the target without clipping gets less gain, never a limiter).

Industry targets: Spotify / YouTube / Tidal / Amazon normalize playback to -14 LUFS, Apple Music -16, Deezer -15, EBU R128 broadcast -23. Club / DJ-pool masters typically run -8 to -9 LUFS. A -1 dBTP ceiling is the streaming norm; use -2 dBTP for lossy encodes at or below 128 kbps.

"Only raise quiet tracks" never turns a loud track down. Normalization needs an audio re-encode - pick an audio codec other than copy/none. Off keeps the source loudness exactly as it is.
enc-loudness.title: Loudness normalization (EBU R128)

enc-rate.body:
CRF / CQ (constant quality) spends bits where the picture needs them; lower values are larger and cleaner. Typical CRF is 18-23 for H.264 / H.265, 24-34 for AV1, 28-34 for VP9. Bitrate mode instead targets a delivery cap and predictable file size.

Non-master profiles avoid up-encoding beyond the source bitrate: re-encoding above the original cannot recover detail that was never there, it only wastes space.
enc-rate.title: Rate control: CRF/CQ vs bitrate

enc-video-codec.body:
Choose a codec based on playback support, file size, and encode time. Copy keeps the original video bytes (CRF, bitrate, scaling, speed and tune do not apply); None disables video so the output is audio-only.

H.264 is the compatibility default - larger than newer codecs, but plays almost everywhere. H.265 / HEVC is more efficient than H.264, especially at 4K, but older devices may need help. VP9 fits WebM well and saves bitrate versus H.264, usually with slower software encoding. AV1 is the most efficient option here; expect slower encodes unless hardware is available.
enc-video-codec.title: Video codec

fingerprinting.body:
A fingerprint is a compact acoustic signature computed from the audio itself - not the file name or tags - so a track can be identified even if it's renamed, re-encoded, or a different pressing.

rave-mate uses Chromaprint (the fingerprinter behind AcoustID) to verify which library track each recorded segment really is, which is what makes "matched ✓" trustworthy on your set history.
fingerprinting.title: Audio fingerprinting

icecast.body:
Icecast is an open-source streaming server. rave-mate runs a tiny local receiver that speaks the Icecast protocol, so Traktor's built-in Broadcasting feature can "stream" your set straight to disk on this machine - no internet involved.

Point Traktor at 127.0.0.1 with the port, mount path and password shown here, hit broadcast, and every set lands in your sets folder time-linked to the session recorder's tracklist - jump to any track in the recording from the Publish tab.
icecast.title: Set capture via Icecast

ml-accel.body: auto negotiates the best common hardware tier (AV1/HEVC/H.264 -> software fallback). Pinning a codec only applies when the sending instance can encode it.
ml-accel.title: Codec / hardware tier

ml-budget.body: Per-route video budget. 20 Mbps fits 1080p60 HEVC with headroom on gigabit LAN.
ml-budget.title: Per-route bitrate

ml-fps.body: Caps how many frames per second leave this machine. VJ tools often render at 120+ fps - every frame above the cap is dropped BEFORE capture-copy, encode and encryption, so the cap directly bounds sender CPU. 60 covers every projector and stream; raise it only if you know the far end displays faster.
ml-fps.title: Sender frame-rate cap

ml-height.body: auto = native resolution everywhere EXCEPT the software-x264 fallback, which caps at 1080p (x264 at 4K60 pins every core - a set-killer). Hardware encoders (NVENC/AMF/QSV) handle 4K60 on dedicated silicon, so 4K flows at full res like NDI. Pick a fixed cap only to save LAN bandwidth; 'native' disables scaling even on the x264 fallback.
ml-height.title: Encode resolution cap

midi-learn-controllers.title: Reading your controller (MIDI-learn)
midi-learn-controllers.body:
rave-mate listens to your DJ controller's MIDI and maps each knob, fader and button to a deck or channel, so the overlays show real EQ, filter, trim, fader and play/cue state.

Why learn it from the controller instead of the DJ software? Because most DJ software can't send its mixer state back out. Traktor can (its Add-Out feature), but Rekordbox and Serato can't emit EQ or fader over a virtual MIDI port at all. And Rekordbox can't even emit play/pause cleanly: its play control is a two-way 'Button' whose LED is sent on the SAME MIDI code it listens on, so on a virtual loopback cable the LED feeds straight back into its own input and the deck toggles itself - the play flicker. Your controller has none of these limits: every knob and button already sends MIDI, so we read it at the source.

Add a controller, pick its MIDI input port, then click Learn on a control and move it once.

midi-in-port.title: MIDI input port
midi-in-port.body:
The controller (or virtual port) rave-mate reads.

On Windows a hardware MIDI input can normally be opened by only ONE application at a time (the legacy winmm MIDI stack is exclusive). So if your DJ software already has the controller open, rave-mate can't also open it here - and vice versa. Three ways around it: use a controller whose driver is multi-client, use the new open-source Windows MIDI Services (MIDI 2.0, native multi-client), or open the controller in rave-mate and route it onward with THRU (below).

midi-thru.title: THRU - share one controller with your DJ software
midi-thru.body:
Because Windows lets only one app open a hardware MIDI input, opening the controller in rave-mate would normally lock your DJ software out of it.

THRU solves that: rave-mate opens the controller and re-sends every message it receives to a loopMIDI port. Point your DJ software's controller mapping at that loopMIDI port and it still gets everything, exactly as before, while rave-mate reads it too. In other words rave-mate becomes the splitter - you do NOT need MIDI-OX or any other router.

Leave THRU off if your controller's driver is multi-client, or if you're on Windows MIDI Services - then both apps can open the hardware directly and no re-routing is needed.

Best THRU target (needs the loopMIDI driver): the rave-mate one-way port. Your DJ software sees an input-only port named 'rave-mate' - there is NO matching output endpoint, so the app's automatic LED echo (rekordbox mirrors every indicator's MIDI IN code back out) has nowhere to loop and it can never react to its own feedback. Select 'rave-mate' as the MIDI device in the DJ software.

With the ravemidi kernel driver installed, 'ravemidi driver' is the best THRU choice: the driver taps the controller in the kernel (forwarding survives rave-mate closing and reboots) and it repairs misbehaving devices - some controllers, e.g. NI Komplete Kontrol keyboards, re-deliver their whole MIDI history with every event, breaking MIDI-learn in any app reading them directly. The driver forwards each message exactly once, so even those controllers work cleanly.

midi-learn-grid.title: The learn grid
midi-learn-grid.body:
One row per control, one column per channel/deck. Click a cell, then move that exact control on your hardware - the first knob-turn or button-press binds it, and the cell then shows the captured MIDI (e.g. CC24). Click the x to clear it, or click a bound cell to re-learn.

Continuous controls (EQ, filter, trim, fader) are captured as Control Change and scaled to 0-100%. Buttons (play, cue) are captured as Notes. A binding remembers the exact MIDI channel and code, so two different controllers can reuse the same numbers without clashing, and all of them feed the same set of decks.

midi-bridge.title: DJ bridge (control from a paired PC)
midi-bridge.body:
Optional. Lets a paired rave-mate instance drive THIS machine's DJ software over MIDI - e.g. a booth operator nudging the DJ's EQ from another PC.

It uses TWO loopMIDI ports on purpose. A paired instance's control is written to the OUT port your DJ software reads; the DJ software's own output (where it has any) is read back on the IN port. Keeping the DJ app's read and write on two DIFFERENT loopback cables is what prevents a self-loop - the same single-port feedback that makes Rekordbox's play button flicker. Your own instance never re-sends MIDI to the port it reads; the bridge only ever carries a peer's control.

app-updates.title: How rave-mate updates itself
app-updates.body:
rave-mate checks its release feed for a newer build every 5 minutes - a tiny manifest download; the request sends no data about you, it only fetches a JSON file. When a new version appears you are notified exactly once per version, here and via a tray balloon.

Channels: every build is locked to the channel it was built from - nightly (rolling build of the latest development tip), alpha (pre-release tags), beta (staging) and production. A build only ever updates within its own channel, so a nightly install stays nightly.

Verification: the feed manifest is signed with the project's Ed25519 release key embedded in this binary - a manifest not signed by that key is rejected outright. Every downloaded file must additionally match its SHA-256 checksum from the signed manifest, and official Windows binaries are Authenticode code-signed. If any check fails the download is discarded and nothing is installed - there is no override.

Steps: 'Download' fetches the new build next to the current one and verifies it (nothing is replaced yet). 'Install' atomically swaps the verified build over the running program - you keep using the old version until you restart. 'Restart to apply' relaunches rave-mate on the new version; a rollback copy (.old) is kept until the next successful start.

motion-studio.body:
Plays back VR motion takes recorded from your headset (head + controllers + any full-body trackers, captured from the wrist menu). The preview shows the skeleton in 3D with the head's travel as a violet trail.

Two live outputs: VMC streams the take as raw tracking devices to a VTuber renderer (VSeeFace, Warudo, VNyan) which does the IK and animates your avatar - this is the real playback path. OSC trackers feed VRChat's full-body tracking, but VRChat always drives head and hands from your live HMD and controllers, so a recorded take cannot puppet your VRChat avatar - export a Unity .anim for that and drive it from the avatar's Animator.

Avatars (.vrm) imported here replicate automatically to your paired rave-mate instances.
motion-studio.title: Motion studio

network-graph.body:
Live send/receive rates over the last 2 minutes.

PEER is the encrypted LAN link to your other paired rave-mate machines (library sync, remote control, media routes). API is traffic to rave.page itself - live-set ingest, uploads, artwork. SESSION totals count everything since the app started.

Spikes during a live set are normal: each confirmed track pushes a now-playing update, and set capture streams continuously.
network-graph.title: Network throughput

obssync-deadband.body: How far out of step (in frames) a source may drift before rave-mate corrects it. A small dead band avoids constant micro-jumps that look like stutter. ~2 frames is a good start.
obssync-deadband.title: Dead band

obssync-fps.body: Your project frame rate. Used only to turn the dead band from frames into milliseconds.
obssync-fps.title: Project frame rate

obssync-mediasync.body: Locks a video/media source in OBS to a shared clock so it plays in step across machines. Start the clock, pick the media source(s), and rave-mate nudges each one to stay on time.
obssync-mediasync.title: OBS media sync

obssync-restart.body: If a source is more than this many ms off, rave-mate restarts it and seeks straight to the target instead of nudging - for big jumps (a source that ended, or was just enabled).
obssync-restart.title: Restart threshold

perf-graph.body:
CPU (top) and RAM (bottom) over the last 2 minutes. APP is rave-mate alone - including its worker subprocesses - SYS is the whole machine.

rave-mate keeps heavy work (transcoding, fingerprinting, media routes) in supervised child processes with bounded buffers, so APP staying flat while SYS climbs means some other program is the load. If APP itself climbs and stays high, check the Logs tab and consider disabling unused features in Settings - disabled features own no ports, goroutines, or subprocesses.
perf-graph.title: System performance

rtsp-passthrough.body: If the source already delivers H.264 (many IP cams, an OBS RTMP feed), copy it through untouched - zero quality loss and near-zero CPU. Leave off for screen capture or non-H.264 sources; they are encoded with zero-latency x264.
rtsp-passthrough.title: H.264 pass-through

rtsp-why.body: VRChat can't receive Spout or NDI, but its AVPro video player accepts rtspt:// (RTSP over TCP) with roughly half a second of delay - the fastest local path into a world. This replaces the usual OBS -> RTMP -> MediaMTX relay chain with one built-in server. Needs ffmpeg (install it under Library & media).
rtsp-why.title: Why RTSP?

session-recorder.body:
Watches your decks and writes a tracklist of what you actually played, with per-track timestamps.

A track only counts once it has played for the confirm threshold - quick previews, tag checks and false starts are filtered out. The result is the set history in the Publish tab, where each entry can be linked to captured audio, OBS recordings, and fingerprint-verified track identities.
session-recorder.title: Session recorder

tc-artnet.body: Art-Net TimeCode is timecode over the network (UDP) for lighting consoles and nodes - grandMA-class desks chase it directly. Default sends to everyone on the LAN (broadcast, port 6454); enter host:port to target one console. Resolume ignores this - use LTC for Resolume.
tc-artnet.title: Art-Net TimeCode

tc-ltc.body: LTC (Linear TimeCode) is timecode as an AUDIO signal - the classic SMPTE format. Pick an audio output here, route it into a virtual audio cable (e.g. VB-CABLE), and select that cable as the timecode input in the receiver. Resolume Arena's SMPTE input only accepts LTC, so this is the output to use for it. Over a real cable it also feeds hardware on another machine.
tc-ltc.title: LTC (Linear TimeCode)

tc-ltc-level.body: Output level in dBFS (decibels below digital full scale). -3 dBFS is the broadcast norm for LTC - loud enough to decode reliably, with headroom against clipping. Lower it if the receiver's input meters clip.
tc-ltc-level.title: LTC output level

tc-mtc.body: MTC (MIDI Time Code) is timecode over MIDI - for sequencers, DAWs and show-control software that chase MIDI (e.g. Reaper, Cubase, QLab). Create a virtual MIDI port with loopMIDI (or Windows MIDI Services loopback), pick it here, and set the receiver to sync to MTC on that port.
tc-mtc.title: MTC (MIDI Time Code)

tc-rate.body: Frames per second of the clock. Pick what the RECEIVER is configured for - both sides must match. 25 is the norm in PAL/EBU regions, 30 and 29.97 drop-frame in NTSC regions, 24 for film. 29.97 drop-frame skips two frame NUMBERS each minute (except every 10th) so the display stays true to the wall clock - no audio/video is dropped.
tc-rate.title: Frame rate

tc-start.body: Where the clock starts counting. A fixed timecode (e.g. 00:00:00:00) is normal for shows; 'time of day' jams the clock to your wall time, handy when several systems should agree on real-world time.
tc-start.title: Start position

tc-timecode.body: SMPTE timecode is a running clock (HH:MM:SS:FF - FF = frame number) that keeps separate software and gear in sync. rave-mate generates one master 'house' clock and sends it out in up to three formats at once; anything listening chases it, on this machine or another one on the network.
tc-timecode.title: SMPTE timecode

timing-graph.body:
Round-trip time to each paired machine on your LAN, in milliseconds, over the last 2 minutes.

RTT is how long a message takes to reach the peer and come back. Single-digit values are typical for wired LAN; Wi-Fi hovers higher and jitters. Sustained spikes usually mean a busy network or a machine going to sleep - remote control and media routes will feel it before anything else.
timing-graph.title: Peer latency (RTT)

trim-editor.body:
Cut the dead air off a recording without touching the original: pick an IN and OUT point and export the kept range as a new file - the source is never modified.

Set the range by dragging the top (IN) / bottom (OUT) edges of the waveform, typing exact times, or Set IN / Set OUT at the current playhead. The Auto-trim menu does it for you: Tracklist bounds snaps to the first track start and last track end from the session recorder; Detect music end runs ffmpeg silence detection over the head and tail; Last fader down uses the exact moment you pulled the fader at the end of the set.

Export: "Lossless Remux" is instant - it copies the streams without re-encoding, but cuts snap to the nearest keyframe (a video cut may start up to a few seconds early). Pick a real encode preset for frame-exact cuts at the cost of a re-encode. For an aligned audio+video pair, "Both (aligned)" cuts the two files at the same real-world moment so they come out content-identical.
trim-editor.title: Trim editor

vrchat-announcement.body:
A VRChat group has one pinned announcement and a feed of posts. Posting a new announcement replaces the current one; posts stack up as a feed and can be deleted individually.

Both require the group-announcement-manage permission - group owners always have it, other members get it through a role. "Send notification" pushes it to members' VRChat notifications, so use it sparingly.
vrchat-announcement.title: Announcement vs. posts

vrchat-presence.body:
Your status controls how visible you are in-game: join me lets friends join your instance directly, active is the everyday default, ask me hides your location so people must request, and busy suppresses invites and notifications entirely.

The status message (32 characters) shows under your name in menus - handy for plugging tonight's set. Changes here apply to your real VRChat account immediately.
vrchat-presence.title: VRChat presence

wave-nav.body:
The waveform is the seek surface: click anywhere to jump there, scroll the mouse wheel to zoom around the cursor (up to 50×), and drag to pan while zoomed. + / − / Fit do the same from the buttons. Violet lines are track starts from the session tracklist, amber is the last fader-down, and colored lines on library tracks are your DJ cue points.

The two chips overlaying the waveform teach as you go: the left one shows the source encoding (hover for codec, sample rate, bitrate and file size), the right one the track's integrated loudness (hover for the full EBU R128 story - integrated vs momentary, streaming targets, true peak). The readout next to the zoom buttons follows your cursor with the time and the momentary loudness at that exact position.

In edit mode the strip gains three pointer lanes: the top edge drags the IN handle, the bottom edge drags OUT, and the middle stays click-to-seek - so you can audition and trim without ever leaving the waveform.
wave-nav.title: Waveform navigation

cue-edit.title: Cue editor — keys & mouse
cue-edit.body: ←/→ move the beat cursor by one beat; Shift+←/→ jump by the beat-jump size; Shift+↑/↓ change that size (1–64 beats). T or Enter drops a DROP marker at the cursor; Shift+T / Shift+Enter removes the nearest one. Drops persist to the library AND into the file tag (MP3/FLAC), so they survive re-imports and machine moves. Mouse: click the waveform to move the cursor (beat-snapped); drag to rubber-band-select cues — save a selection as a named pattern, anchored at the nearest drop. Keys work only in this view while the window is focused, never while typing in a field. In the Collection list, ↑/↓ walk tracks. Hold SPACE to audition from the cursor — release pauses with the decoder parked on the cursor, so the next press starts instantly; after a while idle the engine lets the file go on its own. Ctrl+Z reverts the last edit (grid nudge runs count as one) — press it again to redo. Ctrl+←/→ shifts the whole beatgrid by 10 ms for manual alignment (Ctrl+Shift = 1 ms; hold for continuous travel) — slow enough to land the grid exactly on a beat. Numbers along the top of the waveform show the beat distance between neighbouring cues and drops. Tick checkboxes in the list to mass-apply the assigned patterns via the bar below. Mouse: left-click moves the beat cursor, right-click adds a memory cue, Shift+right-click adds a drop, Ctrl+right-click removes markers at that beat. Grid nudges move cues and drops along with the grid. Drag selects drops as well as cues; click a marker to select just it, Ctrl+click toggles single markers in and out of the selection, and Del (or Backspace) deletes every selected cue and drop in one go — library, change journal and file tag all follow.

k.step: Move the beat cursor one beat
k.zoomKeys: Zoom in / out on the beat cursor (hold for continuous)
k.addDrop: Add a DROP marker at the cursor
k.deleteSel: Delete every selected cue and drop
k.undo: Undo the last cue edit (press again to redo)
k.audition: Hold to audition from the cursor; release pauses — the next press restarts instantly
k.nudge: Nudge the whole beatgrid 10 ms — cues + drops follow (disabled on verified grids)
k.listNav: Walk tracks in the Collection list
k.click: Move the beat cursor to the nearest beat (even onto a marker) and select any marker there
k.ctrlClick: Toggle a cue/drop in or out of the selection
k.rclick: Add a memory cue at that beat
k.addCue: Add a memory cue at the beat cursor
k.crclick: Remove cue + drop markers at that beat
k.prep: Add the track to the preparation playlist
k.prepRemove: Remove it again (only when it's already in — a toast reminds you)

midi-drv-filter.title: Fan-out message filter
midi-drv-filter.body: Message classes the driver drops on the DJ-facing port only (rave-mate still sees everything). Keyboards send aftertouch (channel pressure) with every keypress on every key - if your DJ software's MIDI-learn catches that instead of the note, the binding fires on ANY key and again on release. Filtering aftertouch, active sensing and clock keeps learn clean; leave pitch bend and poly pressure on if you map tempo sliders or pressure pads.

led-feedback.title: LED-feedback test
led-feedback.body:
Sends a short, recognizable burst toward your controller: Note-On messages sweep across notes 36–51 with rising velocity (about one every 50 ms), then everything is switched off again — under two seconds total. Watch the hardware: pads, keys or buttons in that range should light up and go dark again.

The reported count comes from the kernel driver's wire trace: each 'feedback out' entry is one message the driver actually wrote to the device's MIDI input. A full count proves the whole path (app → driver → device) works. Note: some controllers ignore plain MIDI Note-On LEDs — they expect a proprietary mode, a specific channel or velocity map, or HID — so dark LEDs with a full count still mean the transport is fine.

account-bridge.title: rave.page account bridge
account-bridge.body:
The LAN peer link only reaches machines on the same network. This bridge reaches this PC from anywhere - a laptop on tour, the rave.page web app on your phone - by meeting through your rave.page account.

rave.page is only a meeting point. It knows which of your devices are online and passes sealed blobs between them; it cannot read them. The two devices run their own key exchange, prove their identities to each other with the long-term keys they generated locally, and then encrypt everything end-to-end (AES-256-GCM). The server sees ciphertext and byte counts, never a track name, a command, or a token.

Getting in is gated by an authenticator app, not by your rave.page password. You link an authenticator to THIS PC; the secret is generated here, sealed here, and checked here. rave.page never sees it, so a breach of rave.page cannot let anyone in. The first time a device connects it must present a valid 6-digit code. That proves you are holding the authenticator, which authorizes the pairing - it is the remote equivalent of comparing the pairing digits on two screens side by side.

After that first code, the two devices remember each other's keys and this PC hands the caller a one-time key of its own, so you are not typing codes all day. That key is rotated every time it is used, expires after 7 days of not being used, and can be revoked from this screen at any moment. Revoking it forces that device to present a code again.

The gate is deliberately independent of rave.page: the same code-then-key flow is what a future direct PC-to-PC link will use, with no account involved at all.

bridge-local-studio.title: Local Studio over the bridge
bridge-local-studio.body:
Local Studio is the channel that lets the rave.page web app drive this machine - browse your drives, transcode, run automations, control OBS. Normally the browser must be running ON this PC, because the channel is a loopback connection that never leaves the machine.

Turn this on and the exact same channel is offered over the account bridge instead, so the web app can drive this PC from any browser you are signed in on. The protocol is not changed or weakened for this: it is the same key exchange, the same per-message signature, and the same check that both ends belong to the same rave.page account.

What is added is a layer underneath. Before Local Studio says a word, the bridge builds an encrypted tunnel and makes the caller pass the access gate above. That ordering matters: Local Studio's handshake carries an access token, and on a loopback socket that is harmless, but across a relay it would be handing your token to the server. Inside the tunnel it is ciphertext.

Leave this off if you only ever use the web app on this PC - the loopback channel already covers that, and there is no reason to be reachable from outside.

midi-mapping.title: Control rave-mate with your DJ controller
midi-mapping.body: Map any pad, button, knob or endless encoder on your MIDI controller to rave-mate actions: browse the collection, open a track in the cue editor, move the playhead, hold-audition from the cursor, drop markers and nudge the beatgrid - hands on hardware, eyes on the waveform. Click Learn next to an action, touch the control on your device, done. Actions are view-scoped: cue-editor actions only fire while the editor is open, library actions only on the collection list, so one pad can safely mean different things per view. For knobs and encoders pick the value encoding in the row that appears after learning: "absolute knob" for regular potentiometers, one of the relative modes for endless encoders (check your controller manual - two's complement is the most common), plus a sensitivity (ticks per step) and a reverse switch. Mappings are organized into per-device profiles: the device you touch during Learn owns the new mapping, so two controllers can drive the same action with different controls (or different actions with the same CC number). Each device section can be paused as a whole, copied onto another controller (modes and sensitivity survive, only the device changes), or cleared. Mappings learned before profiles existed live under "Any device" and keep firing from every controller.

stream-why.title: VRSL video stream
stream-why.body:
Streams your live DMX lighting into VRChat as video. rave-mate renders the DMX universes into a VRSL pixel grid, encodes it with ffmpeg, and pushes it over RTMP (or WHIP) to a transcode service (VRCDN, Twitch, or your own) that serves it to the headset. The world plays that video back and decodes the grid into lights - no Spout/NDI/OBS relay needed.

Standard mode emits a stock VRSL grid that lights any VRSL world. Extended mode is a superset: it adds 16-bit precision, an integrity header and a liveness counter that a rave.page world decodes, while a stock VRSL world still reads it as plain 8-bit. Keep the whole chain LINEAR - the pixels are raw light values, not a gamma-encoded picture.

auto-watch-dir.title: The folder this automation watches
auto-watch-dir.body:
Every automation is anchored to one folder. Two things can start a run over it: a file arriving (rave-mate watches the folder while the automation is enabled), or a schedule sweeping the folder's current contents on a timer.

The folder is also a safety boundary. The delete step only ever erases the recording its run started from, and refuses outright unless that file is inside this folder.

Subfolders are not included. Both the arrival watcher and a scheduled sweep look only at the files sitting directly in this folder - a recording one level down never starts a run. Point it at the folder your recordings actually land in (the recorder's sets folder, or your OBS output folder).

auto-match-exts.title: Which file types to act on
auto-match-exts.body:
A comma-separated list of file extensions, e.g. ".wav, .flac". Leave it empty to accept any file.

Case and the leading dot do not matter - "WAV" and ".wav" are both understood and stored the same way. This is matched against the file's extension only, never its contents, so a mislabelled file is taken at face value.

Worth setting even when the folder only ever holds recordings: it keeps the chain off the stray sidecar files (cue sheets, .part/.tmp files a recorder writes while still running) that would otherwise trigger a pointless run.

auto-match-pattern.title: Filename pattern (regular expression)
auto-match-pattern.body:
An optional regular expression matched against the file name (not the full path). Leave it empty to accept any name.

It is a search, not a full-string match: "live" matches "my-live-set.wav". Anchor it if you mean the whole name - "^set_" matches names starting with "set_", "\.wav$" only names ending in .wav.

The syntax is RE2 (Go's regexp). It deliberately has no backreferences or lookaround, which is what makes it immune to catastrophic backtracking - it cannot hang the daemon on a pathological name.

If the pattern does not compile it is treated as matching nothing, so the automation quietly stops firing rather than acting on the wrong files. The editor refuses to save an invalid pattern for that reason.

auto-min-age.title: Minimum age (days)
auto-min-age.body:
Only act on files at least this many days old, measured from the file's last-modified time. 0 turns the gate off.

This is built for scheduled sweeps - "archive recordings older than 30 days", "delete raw sets after 90 days". Pair it with a schedule and a move, copy or delete step.

It is almost never what you want on a file-arrival trigger: the watcher fires the moment a recording lands, and a file that was written seconds ago can never be days old, so any age gate above 0 makes a watch-triggered automation do nothing at all. Set an age here and the automation effectively becomes schedule-only.

If the file's timestamp cannot be read, the gate fails closed - the file is skipped rather than deleted or archived on a guess.

auto-trim-silence.title: Trimming the silence off a recording
auto-trim-silence.body:
Recordings usually start before the music does - the recorder is armed while you are still setting up. This step measures how long that silence lasts and re-encodes the file starting after it.

The threshold is the level, in dBFS, below which audio counts as silence. -50 dB is a good default: it ignores room tone, hiss and the noise floor of a mixer, but stops at the first real sound. Raise it (towards 0) if a noisy input keeps the trim from finding the start; lower it if a quiet intro is being cut off.

Minimum silence is how long a quiet stretch must last before it counts. This is what stops the trim from stopping at a single click or a moment between tracks. 2 seconds is the default.

Trim the start and Trim the end are independent, and both are on by default. Turn the end off to keep everything after the last track - useful when the crowd noise or an outro you want is quiet enough to read as silence. Turn the start off and only the tail is cut. With both off the step finds nothing to do and skips itself.

If the recording turns out to have no silence worth cutting at either end, the step skips rather than re-encoding the file for nothing, and the run is reported as partial.

Because the file has to be re-encoded to be cut, this step uses a transcode preset like the transcode step does. Leave the preset alone and it uses "remux", which cuts without touching the audio itself - no quality is lost.

auto-rename-buffer.title: Matching a recording to a booked event
auto-rename-buffer.body:
To name a recording after the gig it came from, rave-mate looks up your booked rave.page events around the file's timestamp. This window is how far, in minutes, it is allowed to look.

The default is 180 minutes (3 hours), which is deliberately generous: a set recorded at 02:00 still belongs to the event that started at 23:00 the night before, and a file's timestamp is when the recording finished, not when the gig began.

Narrow it if you play several venues in one night and the wrong event keeps winning. If no event matches at all, the rename still happens - the venue and event parts of the name fall back to "no-event" rather than leaving the file untouched.

auto-rename-template.title: Filename template
auto-rename-template.body:
How the new file name is built. The default is {YYYY-MM-DD}_{venueSlug}_{eventSlug}{ext}.

Available placeholders: {YYYY-MM-DD} the event date, {venueSlug} the venue, {eventSlug} the event, {originalBasename} the original file name without its extension, and {ext} the original extension including the dot.

Always end with {ext} unless you have a reason not to - an extension is how every other program on your machine knows what the file is. Forward slashes in the template create subfolders under the watch folder, so "{YYYY-MM-DD}/{eventSlug}{ext}" files each gig into its own dated folder.

Anything not a placeholder is used literally. Characters a file name cannot contain are replaced automatically, so a venue called "AC/DC Bar" will not create a stray folder.

auto-loudness.title: Overriding the preset loudness
auto-loudness.body:
Turn this on to normalize loudness with the settings below instead of whatever the preset carries. Leave it off and the preset's own loudness settings apply, exactly as they are.

There is deliberately no "force off" here: this switch can only replace a preset's loudness settings, never disable them. If you want a step that does not normalize at all, point it at a preset that does not normalize.

The integrated target is the loudness the whole file is brought to, in LUFS. -14 is the streaming standard, -23 is the EBU R128 broadcast standard. The true-peak ceiling caps the loudest instantaneous sample in dBTP; -1 leaves headroom so that lossy encoders (which can overshoot on decode) do not clip.

"Only raise quiet tracks" makes it a one-way move: a file already at or above the target is left alone instead of being turned down. Useful for a mixed archive where you want the quiet recordings lifted without touching the ones that are already right.

Normalization is one whole-file volume change, not compression - the dynamics are untouched. It is measured in one pass and applied in a second, so it costs a full read of the file.

auto-delete-action.title: The delete step
auto-delete-action.body:
Erases the recording the chain started from - the file the watcher picked up, the sweep found, or you handed to Run now. It is deliberately NOT whatever the step before it produced: a transcode output or an archived copy survives the delete.

That is what makes transcode + delete mean "convert the recording, then drop the source" - the MP3 stays, the WAV goes. Put a move in the middle and you get the shape most people want: transcode + move-to + delete converts the recording, files the new MP3 into your library folder, and clears the source WAV out of the watch folder. copy-to + delete is the archive shape: copy the recording somewhere else, then clear it out of the working folder. Paired with a minimum age and a schedule, that is a self-maintaining archive.

What the editor will not save is a chain that relocates the recording ITSELF and then deletes it. move-to + delete is rejected: with nothing produced yet, the move takes the recording out of the watch folder, so the delete behind it has nothing left to erase and nothing in its place. Rename from event + delete is rejected for the same reason - the rename gives the recording a new path, and delete only ever erases the file the chain started from. copy-to + move-to + delete is rejected too: a copy does not move the working file, so the move still takes the original. The fix is either a producing step first (transcode or trim-silence - after it, a move relocates that NEW file and the delete clears the source behind it), or copy-to instead of move-to, which leaves the original in place for the delete to clear.

A chain the editor accepts can still refuse at run time, because delete only erases the recording if a new file was actually produced to survive it. If trim-silence finds no silence worth cutting - an Icecast capture that starts on the first beat, or a set you already topped and tailed - it produces nothing, and the delete behind it refuses rather than leaving you with no copy at all: the recording stays and the run is reported partial. Skipping the transcode or trim yourself in a manual run does the same. A chain with no producing step at all - delete on its own, or copy-to + delete - is taken at its word: that is an explicit purge, and it runs.

Delete must be the last step. It consumes the chain's input file, so any step after it would be working on a file it was never handed.

The delete is confined to this automation's watch folder, and the recording has to still be there when the step runs. If it is not - outside the folder, or already relocated by an earlier step - the delete refuses and the run is reported as failed rather than erasing something else instead.

This is permanent: the file does not go to the recycle bin, and there is no undo. A delete as the only step, on a watch trigger, erases every matching file the moment it appears - which is occasionally what you want, and otherwise a very bad afternoon.

auto-sch-kind.title: What starts a scheduled run
auto-sch-kind.body:
A schedule re-runs one automation over the files already sitting in its watch folder. Where the file-arrival trigger reacts to one new file, a schedule sweeps: every file directly in the folder that passes the match rules gets the full action chain, one after another. It does not look inside sub-folders.

There are four triggers. Every few minutes repeats on a fixed gap counted from the last run, so it drifts off the clock - 60 minutes starting at 14:37 fires at 15:37, not on the hour. Daily fires once a day at a wall-clock time. Cron is the escape hatch for everything else: specific weekdays, several times a day, one day a month. When the computer goes idle fires once each time you leave the machine alone long enough, and re-arms when you come back - the natural home for heavy transcodes.

A missed fire is not made up later. If the computer is asleep or rave-mate is closed at the moment a daily or cron schedule was due, that run is simply skipped.

The schedule has its own Enabled switch, separate from the automation's, and both have to be on for anything to happen. Switching the automation off stops it entirely - arriving files and schedules alike. Switching only the schedule off leaves the automation reacting to arriving files, without the recurring sweep.

auto-sch-interval.title: Every N minutes
auto-sch-interval.body:
How long to wait between sweeps, in minutes. The gap is counted from the last run rather than the clock: 60 here means "an hour after the last one", not "on the hour". If you need it on the hour, use a daily or a cron trigger instead.

Left blank this becomes 60. It is deliberately not left at 0 - the scheduler reads 0 as "as fast as possible" and would sweep the folder every single minute.

Sweeps do not stack up. A tick that arrives while the previous sweep is still working is dropped, so a chain slower than its interval just means fewer sweeps, never two at once over the same files. Even so, prefer a gap comfortably longer than the work takes - a transcode chain over a folder of long recordings can outlast a five-minute interval easily.

auto-sch-cron.title: Cron expressions
auto-sch-cron.body:
Five fields separated by spaces: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. Each is either * (every value), a single number, a list (1,15), a range (9-17), or a step (*/15, or 9-17/2).

Examples: */15 * * * * every 15 minutes · 0 9 * * 1-5 at 09:00 on weekdays · 30 2 1 * * at 02:30 on the first of the month · 0 4 * * 0 at 04:00 on Sundays.

Ranges are minute 0-59, hour 0-23 (there is no AM/PM), day-of-month 1-31, month 1-12, and day-of-week 0-6 from Sunday, where 7 also means Sunday. Names like MON or JAN are not supported - use numbers. Neither are the ?, L and # extensions some other cron dialects have.

The classic trap: when you restrict BOTH day-of-month and day-of-week, a run fires if EITHER matches. 0 0 1 * 1 means "the 1st, and also every Monday" - not "the 1st, but only if it is a Monday".

Resolution is one minute; seconds cannot be expressed. The line under the field is the same parser that runs the schedule, so if it says the expression is valid, that is exactly how it will be read.

auto-sch-idle.title: Firing when the computer is idle
auto-sch-idle.body:
How long, in minutes, the computer has to go untouched before this schedule fires. Idle means no keyboard or mouse input at all - a long video counts as idle, a spreadsheet you keep clicking does not.

It fires once per idle period, not repeatedly. Crossing the threshold starts the run, and it only re-arms after you come back and use the machine again - so a computer left alone all night runs the chain once, not every ten minutes until morning.

Left blank this becomes 10. It is deliberately not left at 0: the scheduler skips an idle schedule that has no threshold, so it would silently never fire.

This is the natural home for the expensive chains - transcoding a night's recordings while you are away costs you nothing. Idle detection reads the system's last-input time, which is Windows-only; on other platforms an idle trigger never fires.

auto-sch-require-idle.title: Require idle (minutes)
auto-sch-require-idle.body:
A condition layered on top of whatever trigger you picked: when the trigger fires, only actually run if the computer has been idle at least this long. 0 turns the condition off.

This is how you keep a schedule off your machine while you are working. "Every 30 minutes, but only if I have been away for 10" waits for a break instead of fighting you for CPU mid-set.

It is a gate, not a trigger: a blocked fire is skipped, never queued. It does not run late when you finally step away - the next tick has to come round again. Pair it with a short interval if you want it to catch the first opportunity, or use the idle trigger if "when I leave" is what you actually mean.

Idle detection is Windows-only. Where the system cannot report it this gate is ignored and the schedule fires as normal.

auto-sch-apps.title: Gating a schedule on running apps
auto-sch-apps.body:
Two optional comma-separated lists of application names. Require: every app named there must be running or the fire is skipped. Skip: if any app named there is running, the fire is skipped. Both are checked against the processes alive at the moment the schedule fires.

The skip list is the useful one. "Skip while Traktor or OBS is running" keeps a heavy transcode from stealing CPU in the middle of a set or a stream - the single best reason to set a condition at all.

Names match case-insensitively, with or without the .exe: Traktor, traktor and Traktor.exe all match the same process. Use the executable's name as it appears in Task Manager, not the window title or the product name on the box.

Like the idle gate these are skips, not queues: a blocked fire never happens, it does not wait for the app to close. Process listing is Windows-only; elsewhere these lists are ignored and the schedule fires as normal.

auto-run-now.title: Running an automation by hand
auto-run-now.body:
Runs this automation's action chain once, right now, over one file you pick - the same chain, steps and settings the watcher and the schedules use.

The difference is what it does NOT do: run now skips the match rules entirely. Extension, minimum size, minimum age and the filename pattern are never consulted, so the chain acts on exactly the file you point it at - even one it would never have picked up on its own. That is the point, and it is how you test a chain or catch a file that arrived while the automation was off. It also means those rules are not protecting you here.

The file does not have to live in the watch folder. One step does care: delete refuses to erase anything outside it.

The run is recorded under Recent runs like any other, marked "manual". A long chain keeps going even if you close this dialog.

mp-loudness.title: Normalizing the exported cut
mp-loudness.body:
Turn this on to normalize the loudness of THIS export with the settings below, instead of whatever the encode preset above carries. It changes the exported file only - the preset itself is not touched, and neither is your recording.

Leave it off and the preset's own loudness settings apply, exactly as they are. There is deliberately no "force off" here: this switch can only replace a preset's loudness settings, never disable them. If you want an export that does not normalize at all, pick a preset that does not normalize.

Normalizing rewrites the audio samples, so it needs an audio re-encode. The default Lossless Remux preset copies the audio untouched - with it selected, nothing will be normalized. Pick an encoding preset (Audio Only Opus/AAC/FLAC, or a video preset with an audio codec).

The integrated target is the loudness the whole cut is brought to, in LUFS. -14 is the streaming standard (Spotify, YouTube, Tidal, Amazon), -16 Apple Music, -23 the EBU R128 broadcast standard; club and DJ-pool masters typically sit around -8. The true-peak ceiling caps the loudest instantaneous sample in dBTP; -1 leaves headroom so lossy encoders (which can overshoot on decode) do not clip.

"Only raise quiet tracks" makes it a one-way move: a cut already at or above the target is left alone instead of being turned down.

This is one whole-file volume change, not compression - the mix and the transients are untouched. It is measured in one pass and applied in a second, so it costs a full read of the exported range on top of the encode. When you export an aligned audio + video pair, each half carries its own override - set both if you want both normalized.

mirror.audioNote: Everything below runs on the remote computer - audio auditioning is disabled there, so nothing plays out loud on it.
mirror.timeout: The peer didn't answer - it may be running an older rave-mate without remote-library support.
mirror.noLink: Peer link unavailable - enable Peers to control a paired instance.
mirror.noPicker: File dialogs can't open remotely - they would pop up on the controlled computer. Navigate with the folder list instead.
mirror.noDesktop: Can't open files, folders, or a browser remotely - they would appear on the controlled computer's desktop.

rce.connecting: Fetching track info from the peer…
rce.fileChanged: The file changed on the peer while it was being copied - try again once it settles.
rce.cacheFail: local cache unavailable - cannot pull the peer's file
rce.localNote: Audio, waveform and every edit run on this computer against a cached copy of the file - nothing plays on {name}. Saving writes the cues, beatgrid and drop markers back into {name}'s library and file tags.
rce.unsaved: Unsaved remote changes - edits stay on this computer until you save.
rce.clean: No changes yet - everything matches the peer's library.
rce.saved: Saved - the peer's library matches this editor.
rce.peerMoved: {name} changed this track's cue data since you fetched it - saving will conflict.
rce.peerMovedToast: Peer edited this track - reload from the peer, or overwrite when you save.

Overwrite makes pattern applies replace this mode's existing cues instead of adding around them. Pads always fill in track order — pad 1 fires the earliest cue, matching left-to-right, top-to-bottom pad rows. Each software remembers its own defaults.

gridfix.calNote: The neural detector has a small systematic phase offset vs your DJ software's grids that varies per file format (decoder delay). Mark trusted grids as verified in the Collection tab and press Calibrate there — the measured per-format bias is subtracted from every fix. Re-calibrate after switching the active model.
gridfix.note: The fixer analyzes each track with the Beat This! neural beat tracker (https://github.com/CPJKU/beat_this), fits a constant grid to the detected beats, and only rewrites a grid when the fit is trustworthy — tracks it cannot fix confidently are collected in a MANUAL_GRIDDING_PREP playlist for hand-gridding instead. Your collection is backed up before any write. Analysis runs at below-normal priority so decks, OBS and recordings are never impaired. Expect roughly 10–40 s per track on CPU; the CUDA build is many times faster on an NVIDIA GPU.
gridfix.cudaHint: The CUDA build of PyTorch (several GB) makes analysis and training many times faster on an NVIDIA GPU. It installs into its own environment, independent of the CPU engine — either can be installed first, and both can coexist.
gridfix.variantBroken: {name} engine environment is broken — remove it, then install again.

gridfixmodel.notImproved: Fine-tune did NOT improve held-out accuracy (F {before} → {after}) — keep the previous model.
gridfixmodel.fewHint: Tip: models learn most from tracks the fixer got wrong — hand-grid tracks from the MANUAL_GRIDDING_PREP playlist, verify them, then train. 20+ verified tracks recommended.
gridfixmodel.note: Training fine-tunes the neural beat tracker on your verified grids in rave-mate's own Python environment, at low priority. A held-out validation split measures accuracy before vs after, so a bad training run can simply be discarded — the active model only changes when you select it.

help.step1: In your DJ software (Rekordbox, Serato, etc.) open its MIDI-mapping screen and enable learn on the control you want to map.
help.step2: Move the matching control here (drag a knob or fader, or hit Sweep for a full 0-127 pass) - your software captures rave-mate's outgoing MIDI and maps it. Repeat per control.
help.step3: Save the mapping in your software. Trim has no overlay yet - it is send-only, there so you can pre-learn it.
help.feedback: For LIVE overlay values, point that same software control's OUTPUT / feedback at the SAME CC. It then echoes its position back on that CC and rave-mate reads it straight into your deck overlays - no extra setup.
help.caveat: Rekordbox supports output/feedback mapping well. Serato's per-control output is limited, and Serato will not treat a generic virtual MIDI port as a Serato controller, so live feedback there is partial.

in.intro: Connect a physical DJ controller and learn each control here - EQ, trim, filter, fader, play, cue - straight off the controller's MIDI. This is how EQ/fader/play state reach the overlays; your DJ software can't emit them over a virtual port. Add more than one controller and they all drive the same decks.
in.empty: No controllers yet - add one, pick its MIDI port, then learn its controls.
in.portInUseShort: Not open - in use by another app
in.portInUseHint: Another program (your DJ software, or the controller's own software such as NI Komplete Kontrol) already holds this MIDI port - Windows allows only one app to read a MIDI input at a time. Close that program, or route the controller through a loopMIDI port: set that port as this controller's THRU and point the other app at loopMIDI instead of the hardware.
in.portInUse: '{port}' is in use by another app - close it, or route the controller through loopMIDI (set it as THRU).
in.drvNotReady: The ravemidi driver hasn't bound the controller yet - wait for the driver status above to show forwarding, then try learning again.

in.thru: THRU to (so the DJ app still gets it)
in.thruClashShort: rave-mate already reads this port - the DJ app can't open it too
in.thruClashHint: You've pointed THRU at a port rave-mate itself reads (its Traktor/Denon map, another controller, or the bridge). Windows lets only one app read a MIDI input, so your DJ software can never open it - the forwarded MIDI goes nowhere it can learn from. Fix: make a SEPARATE virtual cable in loopMIDI (e.g. 'rave-mate THRU'), set it as this controller's THRU, and point your DJ software's MIDI-in at that cable. Keep 'LoopBe Internal MIDI' for rave-mate's own Traktor map.
in.relearn: Click, then move the control to re-learn
in.needPort: Pick this controller's MIDI port first
in.listening: Listening - move {control} for CH{ch} on your controller...
in.learnTimeout: No input captured - try again and move the control
in.cloneName: Show under the controller's own name
in.cloneNote: On (default): the forwarded port is named exactly like your controller, so DJ software that maps by device name (Serato) matches your existing mapping automatically - the driver holds the real device and the identically-named port is the one your DJ app opens. Off: it appears as a separate "… THRU" port (use this if a duplicate name in the MIDI list confuses your setup).
in.driverNote: The kernel driver reads the controller directly and keeps forwarding even when rave-mate is closed or after a reboot. Other apps only ever see the forwarded port above - rave-mate reads the controller through the driver internally and holds no MIDI port at all. It also repairs misbehaving hardware: some controllers (NI Komplete Kontrol keyboards, for example) re-deliver their entire MIDI history with every new event, which breaks MIDI-learn in DJ software - the driver detects the replay and forwards every message exactly once, so such devices stay fully usable.

bridge.intro: Optional: route a paired instance's control out to your DJ software. Peer MIDI is written to the OUT port your DJ app reads; the DJ app's own output (where supported) is read back on the IN port. Needs two loopMIDI ports so the DJ app's read and write never share a port (no self-loop).

out.sub: Where rave-mate SENDS MIDI. Pick the built-in one-way port (DJ software can't echo itself back) or any loopback port your DJ app listens on.

rack.sub: Send-to-learn: put your DJ software into MIDI-learn mode, then wiggle a control here — it sends one clean CC/Note for the app to learn. Nothing streams continuously.

drv.why: Our open-source kernel driver creates one-way virtual MIDI ports: your DJ software sees an input-only port, so it can never re-read its own LED/feedback output (the classic loopback self-echo bug). Optional — without it rave-mate falls back to teVirtualMIDI or loopMIDI two-way ports. It also cleans up quirky hardware: some controllers (e.g. NI Komplete Kontrol keyboards) re-deliver their full MIDI history on every event - the driver dedups the stream so every app gets each message exactly once.
drv.installed: Installed and running — one-way ports are served by ravemidi.
drv.fallback: Not installed — using the teVirtualMIDI fallback (two-way; DJ apps can self-echo).
drv.none: Not installed and no teVirtualMIDI found — one-way ports unavailable (loopMIDI still works, two-way).
drv.testsign: Current builds are self-signed (test-signed): Windows loads them only with test-signing boot mode on and Secure Boot off. A Microsoft-attestation-signed release (no special steps) is in the pipeline.
drv.steps: Install (elevated PowerShell, from the driver package folder — full walkthrough in the driver README):
drv.smartscreen: Windows may warn about self-signed components (SmartScreen / unknown publisher). Expected for open-source builds without an EV certificate — the source and CI builds are public; see the README before proceeding.
drv.managedSub: Forwarding lives in the driver and is synced automatically whenever you change a controller here - no manual sync needed. These buttons are fallbacks.
drv.noneManaged: No managed inputs yet — add controllers above, then sync.
drv.syncedToast: {n} managed inputs written to the driver
drv.needControllers: No enabled controllers with a port to sync.
drv.queryFailed: This driver build has no config plane yet — update the driver to enable managed forwarding.
drv.syncFailed: Config not applied to the driver: {err} - if you just updated rave-mate, update/reinstall the ravemidi driver too, then reboot.
drv.fbBusy: An LED-feedback test is already running.
drv.fbRunning: LED test running — watch your controller…
drv.fbNotBound: LED feedback unavailable: the device's MIDI-IN (render) pin isn't bound yet — the device may have no MIDI input, or another app holds it exclusively. The driver keeps retrying in the background.
drv.fbResult: {out} of {sent} test messages reached the device render pin

uimap.sub: Map controller pads, knobs and encoders to cue-editor, library and navigation actions. Learn, touch a control, play.
uimap.note: Mappings listen on every controller input rave-mate reads (add your device under "Controllers" above). While a Learn capture is armed, the touched control is captured only - it never also fires an existing mapping. VR keybinds (Settings -> VR overlays) share this binding store and are not affected by the toggle above.
